intro.title: Your first query
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A **database** keeps data in **tables**. A table looks like a spreadsheet: each **column** holds one kind of value (a title, a year, a price) and each **row** is one record, such as one book. This course uses **SQLite**, a small database that runs right here in your browser.

You ask a database for data with a **query**, written in **SQL** (Structured Query Language). The simplest query shows a whole table:

```
SELECT * FROM books;
```

`SELECT` says what to show, `*` means "every column", and `FROM books` names the table. The semicolon `;` ends the statement. In CodeQuest the result appears as a table, with the number of rows underneath.

This lesson's database has three tables: `books`, `pets` and `products`. Open **Tables** above the editor to see their columns at any time.

To show only some of the columns, name them instead of `*`. This shows just the title of each book:

```
SELECT title FROM books;
```

SQL keywords are not case-sensitive: `select title from books` works too. Writing keywords in capitals is a common habit that makes them stand out from table and column names. Spaces and line breaks don't matter either, so longer queries are often spread over several lines.

Text after `--` is a **comment**: SQLite ignores it until the end of the line. Use comments to leave notes for people reading your SQL.

```
-- every pet in the clinic
SELECT * FROM pets;
```

You can write several statements one after another. Each one runs in turn and shows its own result. In challenges, the **last** result is the one that is checked.

intro.title: Choosing columns
intro.bodyMarkdown:
To show several columns, list them after `SELECT`, separated by commas:

```
SELECT title, author, year FROM books;
```

The result has the columns in the order you list them, which doesn't have to be the order in the table. `SELECT year, title FROM books` puts the year first.

Put a comma **between** columns, but not after the last one. A missing comma is a common mistake: `SELECT title author FROM books` doesn't give an error, but shows the title in a column called `author`. A comma before `FROM` gives `near "FROM": syntax error`.

**Renaming a column.** `AS` gives a column a different name in the result. It doesn't change the table, only the heading you see:

```
SELECT name AS pet, species AS kind FROM pets;
```

A name with a space in it needs double quotes: `SELECT title AS "Book title" FROM books`. Text values use single quotes (next lesson); names use double quotes.

Why not always use `*`? Naming the columns shows only what you need, in the order you want, and the query keeps giving the same columns even if someone adds a column to the table later.

intro.title: Filtering with WHERE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`WHERE` keeps only the rows that match a condition. It comes after `FROM`:

```
SELECT name, age FROM pets WHERE species = 'dog';
```

SQLite checks the condition for every row and keeps the ones where it is true. Here, that is every dog.

Conditions compare values. `=` means equal (just one `=`), `<>` means not equal (`!=` works too), and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes:

```
SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE year < 1900;
```

Numbers are written as they are: `year < 1900`. **Text goes in single quotes**: `species = 'dog'`. Without quotes, SQLite reads the word as a column name, so `WHERE species = dog` gives the error `no such column: dog`.

Text comparisons are exact and case-sensitive: `'Dog'` is not the same as `'dog'`. Look at how the values are written in the table before you filter on them.

You can filter on a column you don't show. This lists the titles of mystery books, without showing the genre:

```
SELECT title FROM books WHERE genre = 'Mystery';
```

The clauses always come in this order: `SELECT` … `FROM` … `WHERE` ….

intro.title: AND, OR and NOT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
One condition is often not enough. `AND` keeps a row only when **both** conditions are true:

```
SELECT name, age FROM pets WHERE species = 'dog' AND age < 5;
```

`OR` keeps a row when **either** condition is true (or both):

```
SELECT name, species FROM pets WHERE species = 'cat' OR species = 'rabbit';
```

Each side must be a complete condition. `species = 'cat' OR 'rabbit'` doesn't do what it seems to; repeat the column: `species = 'cat' OR species = 'rabbit'`.

`NOT` turns a condition around: `WHERE NOT genre = 'Fantasy'` keeps every book that isn't fantasy (the same as `genre <> 'Fantasy'`).

**Brackets matter.** `AND` is worked out before `OR`, just as `*` comes before `+` in maths. So this query, meant to find cats and dogs older than 5, also lists every dog of any age:

```
SELECT name, species, age FROM pets
WHERE species = 'dog' OR species = 'cat' AND age > 5;
```

SQLite reads it as `species = 'dog' OR (species = 'cat' AND age > 5)`. Brackets make it say what you mean:

```
SELECT name, species, age FROM pets
WHERE (species = 'dog' OR species = 'cat') AND age > 5;
```

When a condition mixes `AND` and `OR`, add brackets even where they aren't needed: the query is easier to read and to get right.

intro.title: IN and BETWEEN
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`IN` checks a value against a list. It is a shorter way to write several `OR`s:

```
SELECT title, genre FROM books
WHERE genre IN ('Fantasy', 'Horror', 'Mystery');
```

That is the same as `genre = 'Fantasy' OR genre = 'Horror' OR genre = 'Mystery'`. The list goes in brackets, with commas between the values.

`NOT IN` keeps the rows whose value is **not** in the list.

`BETWEEN` checks a range. **Both ends are included**: `BETWEEN 1900 AND 1999` keeps 1900 and 1999 too.

```
SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE year BETWEEN 1900 AND 1999;
```

It is the same as `year >= 1900 AND year <= 1999`. `NOT BETWEEN` keeps the values outside the range. Write the smaller value first: `BETWEEN 1999 AND 1900` matches nothing.

`BETWEEN` works for text too, in alphabetical order: `name BETWEEN 'A' AND 'D'` keeps names from A up to the single letter D, so `Daisy` is left out (it comes after `'D'`).

`IN` and `BETWEEN` combine with `AND` and `OR` like any other condition.

intro.title: Matching text with LIKE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`=` only matches text exactly. `LIKE` matches a **pattern** with two wildcards: `%` stands for any number of characters (even none), and `_` stands for exactly one character.

```
SELECT title FROM books WHERE title LIKE 'The %';
```

`'The %'` matches every title that starts with `The` and a space. Put the `%` where the unknown part goes: `'The%'` starts with The, `'%y'` ends with y, `'%war%'` contains war anywhere, and `'____'` (four underscores) is exactly four characters long.

In SQLite, `LIKE` ignores the difference between upper and lower case for the letters A to Z, so `name LIKE 'note%'` matches `Notebook`. (`=` doesn't.)

```
SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%note%';
```

`NOT LIKE` keeps the rows that don't match the pattern.

Without wildcards, `LIKE` is just an equals that ignores case: `species LIKE 'DOG'` matches `dog`. Use `=` when you know the exact value, and `LIKE` when you know only part of it.

intro.title: Missing values: NULL
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Sometimes a value is missing: a book that hasn't been rated yet, a pet with no owner on record. A database stores that as `NULL`, which means "unknown". It is not 0 and not empty text: it is no value at all.

`NULL` follows its own rules. Any comparison with it gives "unknown" instead of true or false, and `WHERE` only keeps rows where the condition is true. So `rating = NULL` never matches anything, not even the books without a rating.

To find missing values, use `IS NULL`; to find the rows that have a value, use `IS NOT NULL`:

```
SELECT title FROM books WHERE rating IS NULL;
```

```
SELECT name, breed FROM pets WHERE breed IS NOT NULL;
```

This rule catches people out with "not" conditions. `WHERE owner <> 'Ana'` leaves out Ana's pets, but it also leaves out the pets with no owner, because comparing `NULL` with `'Ana'` gives unknown. To include them, ask for them too:

```
SELECT name, owner FROM pets WHERE owner <> 'Ana' OR owner IS NULL;
```

In results, CodeQuest shows a missing value as `NULL`.

intro.title: Sorting with ORDER BY
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Without instructions, a database may return rows in any order. Often it is the order they were added, but you can't rely on that. `ORDER BY` sorts the result:

```
SELECT title, year FROM books ORDER BY year;
```

The order is **ascending** (smallest first, A to Z) unless you say otherwise. Add `DESC` for **descending** order, largest first. (`ASC` asks for ascending order explicitly.)

```
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC;
```

Sort by several columns by listing them: the second column only decides the order of rows that are equal in the first. Each column can have its own `DESC`:

```
SELECT title, genre, year FROM books ORDER BY genre, year DESC;
```

You can sort by a column you don't show, and by a name you gave a column with `AS`. Text sorts alphabetically, with capital letters before lower-case ones; in ascending order, `NULL` comes first.

`ORDER BY` goes after `WHERE`: `SELECT` … `FROM` … `WHERE` … `ORDER BY` ….

When two rows tie on every sort column, their order is not fixed. If the order matters, add another column to break ties, such as `ORDER BY price, name`.

intro.title: LIMIT and DISTINCT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`LIMIT` keeps only the first few rows of a result. Together with `ORDER BY`, it answers "top" questions, such as the three most expensive products:

```
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;
```

Without `ORDER BY`, "the first 3 rows" could be any 3 rows, so always sort before you limit.

`OFFSET` skips rows before the limit starts. `LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5` gives rows 6 to 10, which is how apps show results page by page.

```
SELECT title FROM books ORDER BY title LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;
```

`DISTINCT` removes repeated rows from a result. It goes straight after `SELECT`:

```
SELECT DISTINCT species FROM pets;
```

With several columns, `DISTINCT` removes rows where **all** the columns repeat, so `SELECT DISTINCT species, owner` lists each combination once.

The full order of the clauses is now `SELECT` (`DISTINCT`) … `FROM` … `WHERE` … `ORDER BY` … `LIMIT` … `OFFSET` ….

intro.title: Calculated columns
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A column in the result can be a **calculation** instead of a stored value. This shows how much each product's stock is worth:

```
SELECT name, price * stock AS stock_value FROM products;
```

You can use `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, with brackets as in maths. **Always name a calculated column with `AS`**: otherwise its heading is the calculation itself, such as `price * stock`.

**Watch out for whole-number division.** When both numbers are whole, SQLite gives a whole-number answer: `7 / 2` is `3`. If either number has a decimal point, you get decimals: `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`. So `stock / 8.0` keeps the decimals that `stock / 8` drops.

`ROUND(value, 2)` rounds to 2 decimal places, which is handy for money: `ROUND(price * 0.8, 2)`.

`||` joins text together. Numbers can be joined too:

```
SELECT title || ' (' || year || ')' AS label FROM books;
```

`UPPER(text)` and `LOWER(text)` change the case, and `LENGTH(text)` counts the characters. The next section has many more functions.

A calculation can be used in `WHERE` and `ORDER BY` too. In `WHERE`, write the calculation again rather than using its `AS` name: most databases don't allow the name there.

```
SELECT name, price * stock AS stock_value FROM products
WHERE price * stock > 500
ORDER BY stock_value DESC;
```

intro.title: Easy project: Library report
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The library wants a few lists from its `books` table: what it has, the classics, the books still waiting for a rating, and the best-rated ones.

Each challenge is one part of the report. They use what you learned in this section: choosing columns, `WHERE`, `NULL`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` and joining text with `||`.

Try your ideas in the sandbox first. Remember to sort when the order matters, and to give calculated columns the name the challenge asks for.
intro.sandboxCode: SELECT title, author, year, rating FROM books ORDER BY author, title;

challenges.title: Easy: The catalogue
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` and `author` of every book, sorted by author and then by title.
challenges.hint: `ORDER BY author, title`.
challenges.solution: SELECT title, author FROM books ORDER BY author, title;

challenges.title: Easy: The classics
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` and `year` of the books published before 1950, oldest first.
challenges.hint: `WHERE year < 1950 ORDER BY year`.
challenges.solution: SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE year < 1950 ORDER BY year;

challenges.title: Medium: Waiting for a rating
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` of every book that has no rating yet, in title order.
challenges.hint: `WHERE rating IS NULL ORDER BY title`.
challenges.solution: SELECT title FROM books WHERE rating IS NULL ORDER BY title;

challenges.title: Medium: Top five
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `title` and `rating` of the five best-rated books, best first. Books with the same rating go in title order.
challenges.hint: Leave out the unrated books, then `ORDER BY rating DESC, title LIMIT 5`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT title, rating FROM books
WHERE rating IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY rating DESC, title
LIMIT 5;

challenges.title: Hard: Catalogue entries
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show one column called `entry` with each book's title and year in brackets, like `Dune (1965)`, oldest first.
challenges.hint: `title || ' (' || year || ')' AS entry`, then `ORDER BY year`.
challenges.solution: SELECT title || ' (' || year || ')' AS entry FROM books ORDER BY year;

challenges.title: Hard: Best of the imagination
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `genre`, `title` and `rating` of the `Science Fiction` and `Fantasy` books rated 4.5 or higher. Sort by genre, then best rating first, then title.
challenges.hint: `WHERE genre IN ('Science Fiction', 'Fantasy') AND rating >= 4.5 ORDER BY genre, rating DESC, title`.

intro.title: Medium project: Pet clinic

The vet's clinic keeps its patients in the `pets` table. Today you'll prepare the lists the reception desk needs: the check-up list, the records with missing details, weights in pounds, and labels for the appointment board.

Some pets have no breed or no owner recorded, so watch out for `NULL`. One kilogram is about 2.2046 pounds.

This project puts the whole section together: conditions, `IN`, `LIKE`, `ORDER BY` with tie-breakers, calculated columns with `AS`, `ROUND` and `UPPER`.

Give calculated columns exactly the names the challenges ask for, and add tie-breakers where rows could be equal.

challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name`, `category` and `price` of products priced from 5 to 20 that are not stationery, cheapest first.
challenges.hint: `WHERE price BETWEEN 5 AND 20 AND category <> 'stationery' ORDER BY price`.

challenges.title: Medium: Sale tags
challenges.promptMarkdown: For the `electronics` and `bags` products, show the `name`, `price` and the price with 25% off rounded to 2 decimals, called `sale_price`. Highest sale price first.
challenges.hint: `ROUND(price * 0.75, 2) AS sale_price`, `WHERE category IN ('electronics', 'bags')`, `ORDER BY sale_price DESC`.

challenges.title: Hard: Search the shelves
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the `name` and `stock` of the products in stock (above 0) whose name contains the letter `e`, in name order.
challenges.hint: `WHERE stock > 0 AND name LIKE '%e%' ORDER BY name`.
challenges.solution: SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE stock > 0 AND name LIKE '%e%' ORDER BY name;

challenges.title: Hard: The manager's report
challenges.promptMarkdown: Show the category in capitals (called `category`), the `name`, and the stock value (price times stock, called `stock_value`) of the products whose stock is worth more than 300. Highest value first.
challenges.hint: `UPPER(category) AS category`, `price * stock AS stock_value`, `WHERE price * stock > 300 ORDER BY stock_value DESC`.

questions.prompt: Which keeps products priced from 5 to 20, both included?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN includes both ends, smaller value first.

questions.prompt: Why give `price * stock` a name with AS?

choices.label: So the result has a clear heading, like `stock_value`
It saves it in the table

questions.explanation: Without AS, the heading would be the calculation itself.

questions.prompt: What is 25% off 40?
In WHERE, how do you filter on the stock value?
questions.explanation: Repeat the calculation; most databases don't allow the AS name in WHERE.

questions.prompt: Which function turns text into capital letters?
questions.explanation: `UPPER('kitchen')` gives `KITCHEN`.

questions.prompt: Which finds names containing an e?
questions.explanation: `%` on both sides allows anything before and after the e.
